text: A website for Sweet Crumbs Bakery in Pune: menu, cake orders, contact

@CEO The brief fixes scope (menu, cake orders, contact) but leaves three choices that change what the charter can promise. Please decide these so Identity can write the goal, standards and done-when list.
1. How should a customer place a cake order on the site, given it is a single static HTML file with no server?
   Option 1: Online checkout with payment at order time. Consequence: orders are confirmed and paid up front. Risk: needs a payment provider account and external commitments the single-file site cannot handle alone, and delays delivery of the first version.
   Option 2: Order form that opens a WhatsApp chat with the details prefilled. Consequence: orders reach the bakery directly and the site stores nothing. Risk: needs a bakery WhatsApp number, and every order needs manual confirmation.
   Option 3: Order form sent to the bakery's email through a third-party form service. Consequence: orders arrive as structured emails with all fields. Risk: depends on an outside service and an account the Requester must own, and emails can be missed or land in spam.
   Option 4: No form: show phone number and a checklist of what to tell the bakery (size, flavour, date, message). Consequence: simplest to build and keep working. Risk: fewer orders, details arrive incomplete, and out-of-hours enquiries are lost.
2. How should the menu show prices, given the brief does not say whether the bakery wants them public?
   Option 1: Show full prices for every item. Consequence: customers can decide without asking, which cuts enquiries. Risk: the Requester must supply accurate prices, and wrong or outdated prices mislead customers.
   Option 2: Show no prices and invite customers to ask. Consequence: no price upkeep and full control over quotes. Risk: some visitors leave without enquiring, and every sale needs a conversation.
   Option 3: Show 'starting from' prices for cakes and fixed prices for other items. Consequence: gives a budget signal while leaving room for custom cake quotes. Risk: still needs Requester-supplied figures, and customers may expect the 'from' price on custom work.
3. What should the site say about getting cakes to customers in Pune?
   Option 1: Pickup from the bakery only. Consequence: simple order form and a clear address and map in the contact section. Risk: loses customers who want delivery.
   Option 2: Make no fulfilment promise on the site and settle pickup or delivery in the order conversation. Consequence: least content to maintain. Risk: customers are unsure whether the bakery can reach them and may not order.
   Option 3: Delivery within a named list of Pune areas plus pickup. Consequence: order form collects area and address, and the site sets clear expectations. Risk: the Requester must provide the areas, and the list goes stale if the bakery's range changes.

@Identity Decisions: WhatsApp-prefilled order form, 'starting from' cake prices with fixed prices for other items, and named-area delivery plus pickup. The brief is silent on all three, so I chose on the merits. Trade-off accepted: every order needs manual confirmation, and the Requester must supply the WhatsApp number, prices and delivery areas. These are open inputs shown as marked placeholders on the site and must not block done.
1. How should a customer place a cake order on the site, given it is a single static HTML file with no server? Order form that opens a WhatsApp chat with the details prefilled. Consequence: orders reach the bakery directly and the site stores nothing. Risk: needs a bakery WhatsApp number, and every order needs manual confirmation. (It works in a single static file with no server, account or payment provider, reaches the bakery in a channel Pune customers already use, and can be swapped for a different method later.)
2. How should the menu show prices, given the brief does not say whether the bakery wants them public? Show 'starting from' prices for cakes and fixed prices for other items. Consequence: gives a budget signal while leaving room for custom cake quotes. Risk: still needs Requester-supplied figures, and customers may expect the 'from' price on custom work. (It gives customers a budget signal and cuts basic enquiries while leaving room to quote custom cakes, and it needs less upkeep than full prices on every item.)
3. What should the site say about getting cakes to customers in Pune? Delivery within a named list of Pune areas plus pickup. Consequence: order form collects area and address, and the site sets clear expectations. Risk: the Requester must provide the areas, and the list goes stale if the bakery's range changes. (It sets clear expectations for customers and lets the order form collect area and address, and the area list is a single editable block if the bakery's range changes.)

@Adaptation Charter is recorded from the brief and the CEO's three decisions: WhatsApp-prefilled order form, 'starting from' cake prices with fixed prices for other items, and named-area delivery plus pickup. Propose workflows that meet every done-when item; missing facts stay as marked placeholders and do not block done.
@Adaptation Charter valid: statement present, 11 checkable done-when items. Work can start.

@Priority Two workflows build the whole site for 60 of the 100 budget. W1 creates the file with the menu, contact and responsive styling. W2 adds the cake order section, form and WhatsApp link. Every unknown fact is a visible [PLACEHOLDER: ...] marker matching open_inputs, and the remaining 40 stays free for audit fixes.

proposal.name: Single-file base page with menu and contact sections
proposal.goal_gap: No site file exists. Needed: one HTML file naming Sweet Crumbs Bakery and Pune, with grouped menu and contact sections, responsive on phones.
proposal.expected_outcome: One HTML file with inline CSS and JS and no build step. It has a header naming Sweet Crumbs Bakery, Pune. The menu is grouped, with cakes shown as 'starting from' prices and other items at fixed prices. The contact section has address, phone, WhatsApp link and opening hours. Unknown values use the [PLACEHOLDER: ...] marker. It includes a viewport meta tag and a small-screen rule that stacks the sections.
outputs: site.html with header, menu section, contact section, responsive CSS, placeholder markers
proposal.completion_check: The file opens locally without a server. It contains 'Sweet Crumbs Bakery' and 'Pune', a menu section with grouped items, and a contact section with address, phone, WhatsApp link and hours. Cake entries show 'starting from' and non-cake entries show a fixed price or a [PLACEHOLDER: ...] marker. A viewport meta tag and a small-screen media query are present. It has no payment code, no fetch or XHR calls and no storage use.

proposal.name: Cake order section with WhatsApp prefilled form
proposal.goal_gap: No way to order a cake. Needed: a form that opens a prefilled WhatsApp chat, delivery areas in one editable block, and a manual-confirmation notice.
proposal.expected_outcome: A cake orders section in site.html. The form has fields for size, flavour, date, message, pickup or delivery choice, delivery area and delivery address. On submit, script builds a wa.me link with the message text from the fields and opens it. The WhatsApp number is a single marked placeholder constant. The Pune delivery areas sit in one editable block (placeholders if unknown), alongside a statement of delivery within those areas plus pickup. A notice says the bakery confirms every order after the WhatsApp message is sent.
outputs: site.html updated with cake orders section, order form, WhatsApp submit script, delivery area block, confirmation notice
proposal.completion_check: The section is labelled for cake orders and has all required form fields. Submit handler builds a wa.me URL from the field values, with the number as one marked placeholder constant. The delivery area list is a single editable block. The page text states that orders are confirmed by the bakery after the WhatsApp message. The file contains no fetch, XHR, payment code or localStorage/cookie use. The section stacks on small screens.
